headline.en: A plain tune and a styled one are the same notes. The difference is a few small moves, like a scoop up into a note.

detail.en: Down in the Valley, a traditional song, with a scoop into "val-"
Medium volume, the middle of your voice
Stop if anything tightens, tickles or hurts. Don't sing when you're ill; see someone if hoarseness lasts more than two weeks. No app replaces a teacher

text.en: The scoop on its own: start a little below "val-" and slide up into it.
First the line plain, over the chords.
Now the same line with your scoop into "val-". If we don't hear it, try a bigger, slower one.

measures.en: Scored on the scoop and the notes. Listen back to both takes: same notes, different song. Next: the scoop, up close.

headline.en: A scoop slides up into a note from a little below, on purpose. Done well it sounds meant, not missed.

detail.en: A semitone to a third under the note
A flick, or a slow, easy rise
Then hold it steady

text.en: Listen to both, then choose.

why.en: B slid up into the note from below. A started right on it.
A rose into its note; B was straight from the start.

text.en: Three notes at your own pace: start a little below each and slide up into it.
Listen, then sing them back, each with a quick scoop.
Now lazy scoops: a slower, easy rise into each.

measures.en: Scored on the scoops and the notes they land on. Did they sound meant, not missed? Next: the fall-off.

headline.en: A fall-off lets the end of a note drop away. Let the pitch go and keep the breath steady, never a collapse into a creak.

detail.en: The note first, the fall at its end
Hold, then let each end drop away
The pitch falls, the breath doesn't

text.en: Hold each note at your own pace; the fall-off comes when you let go.
Listen, then sing them back, each falling off at the end.
Longer notes: hold, then let each end drop away.
The line's last note, "low", with a fall-off.

measures.en: Scored on the fall-off and the notes. Next: the whole verse, styled.

headline.en: The whole verse with two scoops and two fall-offs, on the long notes and the ends of lines.

detail.en: Into "val-" and "o-"
On "low" and "blow"
Moves mean more when they're rare

text.en: The verse at your own pace first.
After a bar of chords, sing the styled verse.

measures.en: Scored on the moves asked for and the notes. Listen back: did they sound meant? Next: the slide.

headline.en: A slide glides from one note to the next on one breath, through every pitch between. Slow and smooth, it sounds like a sigh with a tune in it.

detail.en: The two notes joined, no gap
Every pitch between, evenly
Stop if anything tightens, tickles or hurts; rest when hoarse

text.en: Slide up a third and back, at your own pace.
Listen, then slide up a third and back down.
A wider slide, a fifth: up and back, smooth all the way.
Now a line with two slides, into "val-" and into "low".

measures.en: Scored on the slides and the notes. Next: the little cry.

headline.en: Country singers add a little cry: a quick flip up into the lighter voice, where it changes gear, and straight back down. Light, never a hard catch.

detail.en: Into the lighter voice, and back

title.en: At the start or inside a note

detail.en: A held note is easiest
Not the sob in it: that part is yours

text.en: A slow practice cry first, at your own pace: the note, a quick step up, and back.
Now quicker, as a cry: listen, then sing three back.
In a song: Down in the Valley's first line with a cry on "low".

measures.en: Scored on the cry and the notes. Next: hear the moves apart.

headline.en: Four moves so far: a scoop, a fall-off, a slide and a cry. Can you tell them apart, and hear when they're too many?

detail.en: Each round has one move
Only your first answer counts
Which one overdid it?

text.en: Listen, then choose.

why.en: A scoop: it rose into "val-" from below.
A fall-off: "low" dropped away at its end.
A cry: a quick flick up inside "ley", and back.
A slide again, from "ley" down into "so".
B put a move on nearly every note. A saved two for the long notes, and they meant more.

measures.en: Scored on the rounds you got right first time. Next: a cowboy song, styled.

headline.en: A cowboy lament, styled: a slide from "not", a light cry on "lone", a scoop into "low" and a fall-off at the end.

title.en: Bury Me Not on the Lone Prairie

detail.en: Words collected in 1910, to The Ocean Burial, George N. Allen's 1839 tune
The slide, the scoop and the fall sit on five-beat notes
A flick, never a hard catch

text.en: The two lines at your own pace first.
After the drone's lead-in, sing the two lines, styled.

measures.en: Scored on the moves asked for and the notes. Listen back: did the long notes carry them? Next: tone colours.

headline.en: The same line can be breathy, bright or twangy. These are tone colours: we can't score them yet, so you'll be the judge.

detail.en: A little air, quiet and close; water nearby
A clear ring from the vowel, never louder
A narrow edge from a light "nyeh", never pressed

text.en: First the line plain, over the chords: the colours come next.

measures.en: Scored on the plain line's notes; the colours that follow are yours to judge. Next: the crooner.

text.en: Breathy first: quiet and close, a little air in the sound, never a whisper. Sing the line, then hear yours beside the guide's. We don't score the tone yet.

description.en: Breathy: quiet and close, with a little air in the sound, like singing to one person.

questions.en: Could you hear air in it?

text.en: Now bright: a clear, forward ring from the vowel and a slight smile, never from more volume. This isn't belting.

description.en: Bright: a clear, forward ring from the vowel and a slight smile, never from more volume.

questions.en: Did it ring without getting louder?

text.en: Now a little twang: a narrow, bright edge, from a light, bratty "nyeh". Never squeezed.

description.en: Twang: a narrow, bright edge, like a light, bratty "nyeh", never squeezed.

questions.en: Pinch your nose and sing it again: did it sound about the same? (If it changed a lot, it was nasal, not twang.)
Did one colour feel most like you? Keep it in mind for Your colour.

headline.en: Crooning became popular when electric microphones arrived in the 1920s: quiet, close singing, a little air in it, and fall-offs at the ends of lines.

detail.en: Poulton and Fosdick, 1861: a little air, quiet and close, never a whisper
Stay quiet; don't push to be heard
Breathy singing dries the voice

text.en: Aura Lee's first two lines at your own pace.
Sing them breathy and close, with a fall-off on "Spring" and on "tree".

measures.en: Scored on the fall-offs and the notes, judged gently: air in the sound makes pitch harder to hear. The tone is yours to judge. Next: the country edge.

text.en: Once more, then hear yours beside the guide's. We don't score the tone yet.

questions.en: Could you hear a little air, not a whisper?
Did you stay quiet, without pushing?

headline.en: A little twang gives country singing its edge: narrow and bright, never pressed. Find it from a light, bratty "nyeh", then add a cry.

detail.en: Light and bratty, like teasing
If pinching your nose changes it a lot, it's nasal, not twang
Twang is bright, never squeezed

text.en: Find the twang first: a light, bratty "nyeh" on the line's notes, at your own pace.
The first line with a little twang and a light cry on "lone".

measures.en: Scored on the cry and the notes. The twang is yours to judge. Next: your colour, your song.

text.en: Once more, then hear yours beside the guide's. We don't score the tone yet.

questions.en: Pinch your nose and sing it again: did it sound about the same? (If it changed a lot, it was nasal, not twang.)

headline.en: Aura Lee's verse in the colour that felt most like you, with two slides from unit 2 and fall-offs at the line ends.

detail.en: Breathy, bright or a little twang
From "bird" and from "him"
On "tree" and "Lea"

text.en: The verse at your own pace first.
After a bar of chords, sing the verse in your colour, styled.

measures.en: Scored on the moves and the notes, judged gently. The colour is yours to judge: listen back. Next: where the moves go.

headline.en: A rule of thumb: moves on the long notes and the ends of lines, plain everywhere else. They mean more when they're rare.

detail.en: Room for a move to be heard
A fall-off or a cry to close
So the moves stand out

text.en: Listen to both, then choose.

prompt.en: Which one styled only the long notes?

why.en: A's moves were on "val-", "ley" and "low", the long ones. B's were on quick notes, where they blur.

prompt.en: Which one saved its move for the last word?

why.en: B's cry came on "low", the line's last word. A's was on "in", near the start.

prompt.en: Which one styled only the long notes?

why.en: B scooped into "o-" and fell off "blow", both long. A's moves were on short notes.

prompt.en: Which one ends with a fall-off?

why.en: A's "blow" dropped away at the end.

measures.en: Scored on the rounds you got right first time.

text.en: Now the line your way: two moves at most, on the long notes.

measures.en: Scored on the notes and any move of yours we heard on a long note. Next: answer the guide back.

headline.en: The guide styles a line its way; you answer the same notes with moves of your own.

detail.en: Then answer with your own
One heard is enough
Two or three, on long notes

text.en: The line plain at your own pace first, so you know its notes.
Listen to the guide's line, then answer it your way.
And the second line.

measures.en: Scored on the notes and any move of yours we heard: never more for more. Next: your way, on a new tune.

headline.en: Beautiful Dreamer's first line, plain on the screen. Style it your way: a scoop, a fall-off, a slide or a cry.

detail.en: Stephen Foster, 1864
Every move from the course
Listen back after each

text.en: The line plain at your own pace first.
After a bar of chords, sing it your way.
Now plain, no moves at all, to hear the difference.
Once more, a different way.

measures.en: Scored on the notes and any move of yours we heard, never more for more. Meant more? We may have missed a small one. Next: your record.

headline.en: Back to lesson 1's song. Then: plain. Now: your record, your way, in your colour.

detail.en: The whole verse, over chords
Two or three moves, where they fit
Stop if anything tightens, tickles or hurts; rest when hoarse

text.en: The verse at your own pace first.
After a bar of chords, sing your record.

measures.en: Scored on the notes and any move of yours we heard. Listen back: then plain, now your record.

text.en: Hear yours beside the guide's plain verse. We don't score the colour yet.

questions.en: Did your moves land on the long notes?
Did your colour stay easy, never pushed?
